messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: assigning to sub vectors
parts:
Hi!

I just found out that I cannot write something like this

segment(big_vector, 5, 10) <- small_vector_of_length_10;

Stan complains that I wrote down a logical statement which is wrong. So I am wondering if I can assign to a sub-vector another vector without a for-loop (and a temporary in my case)?

Many thanks. Almost forgot, it's Stan 2.2.0.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning to sub vectors
parts:
Not yet. The only expressions allowed on the LHS
of an assignment are a variable and optional indices.

In programming language terms, none of the Stan functions produce
lvalues as output within Stan. The only operation that produces
lvalues is indexing a variable.

In the C++ implementation, most functions also do not produce
valid C++ lvalues because of the way Eigen's expression templates
work and our simplified return typing. Because we declare functions
to return Matrix<T,R,C> instances, this causes a copy on return for
any intermediate expression templates. We'll soon be rewriting some of the
matrix auto-diff to take advantage of the expression templates from
Eigen, which has shown some substantial speedups in early prototypes
for matrix functions (factors of 3 or so!). This will in turn make it
easier to have more elaborate lvalues in the Stan language.

I also hope to implement the full R-like array indexing, so you
can write things like:

a[1:3] <- b;

c <- d[1:3,];

e <- f[2:9,13:101];

Probably some time over the next year :-)

- Bob

messages.author: 5a7d96b840c23bef
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning to sub vectors
parts:
Hi Bob,

Now that we have functions and ODE's are not far behind, this feature (assigning to segments or slices of vectors, matrices or arrays) seems like it deserves even higher priority. I keep encountering situations where I want to define functions that return vectors, matrices or arrays. Often those functions are to be applied repeatedly but with varying dimensions of the return value. A typical example would a function to calculate a vector of predicted drug concentrations over multiple observation times for each individual patient in a clinical trial. More often than not the patients differ w.r.t. the number and timing of observations. So far I haven't figured out any good kluges to get around this other than to just make functions that return scalar values and do the calculations separately for each observation time.

Just a friendly nudge....

Thanks,
Bill

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning to sub vectors
parts:
Yes, definitely something we should do. Not to mention the
more ambitious problem of allowing general R/MATLAB-style
slicing syntax (e.g, a[,2:3,5] <- b[6:7,8]).

As much as I'd like to enrich the language, I don't think
this one's even in the top hundred on our to-do list (not
that we're that organized). This one's hard to pass off to
someone else because it changes the notion of lvalue and
rvalue in the language. There's an example for assigning to
rows of matrices, but that's it. So it wouldn't be impossible
for someone outside the core dev team to take it on, it's
more likely something I'll have to do personally.

It would be great if someone wants to volunteer to help with
parsing and code gen. The real bottleneck now is that I'm
about the only one comfortable with that part of the code.

- Bob

messages.author: 5a7d96b840c23bef
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning to sub vectors
parts:
I'm afraid I'm not yet facile enough with the guts of Stan to take it on. In the mean time the following illustrates a rather dirty kluge to work around the limitation. It's a simple linear mixed effects model with slopes and intercepts that differ for each individual. nmax is a hard-coded maximum number of observations per individual. Let me know if you see any serious pitfalls in this approach.

Thanks,
Bill

## Toy problem to test approach to get around inability to assign to
## vector segments
 
functions{
 
  vector yCalc(vector x, real a, real b, int nmax){
    vector[rows(x)] y;
    vector[nmax] res;
 
    y <- a + b * x;
    for(i in 1:rows(x)) 
      res[i] <- y[i];
    for(i in (rows(x) + 1):nmax)
      res[i] <- 0;
    return(res);
  }
 
}
 
data{
  int nobs;
  int nind;
  vector[nobs] y;
  vector[nobs] x;
  int start[nind];
  int end[nind];
}
 
transformed data{
  int nmax;
  nmax <- 12;
}
 
parameters{
  real aMean;
  real bMean;
  real<lower = 0> omegaa;
  real<lower = 0> omegab;
  real<lower = 0> sigma;
  real a[nind];
  real b[nind];
}
 
transformed parameters{
  real yHat[nobs];
  vector[nmax] temp;
 
  for(j in 1:nind){
    temp <- yCalc(segment(x, start[j], end[j] - start[j] + 1), a[j], b[j], nmax);
    for(i in start[j]:end[j])
      yHat[i] <- temp[i - start[j] + 1];
  }
}
 
model{
  aMean ~ normal(0, 10);
  bMean ~ normal(0, 10);
  omegaa ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  omegab ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
 
  a ~ normal(aMean, omegaa);
  b ~ normal(bMean, omegab);
 
  y ~ normal(yHat, sigma);
}

On Sep 16, 2014, at 8:48 PM, Bill Gillespie <bi...@metrumrg.com> wrote:

Let me know if you see any serious pitfalls in this approach.

Yikes --- I see what you're doing and if we had
ragged arrays, your model would be clean as a whistle.

If we had segmented assignment, it'd be a bit cleaner.

Is it really necessary to put everything into one big
vector? Otherwise, I'd think a function to slice each
individual out and sample it would get around all the
reassignment.

for (j in 1:nind)
segment(y, start[j], end[j] - start[j] + 1)
~ normal(a[j] + b[j] * segment(x, start[j], end[j] - start[j] + 1),
sigma);

It's still not pretty. It'd be much nicer if we could write that segment()
as y[start[j] : end[j]].

so I might want to write a function slice an individual out and use it
for both x and y so this could be written as:

for (j in 1:nind)
slice(y,start[j],end[j])
~ normal(a[j] + b[j] * slice(x,start[j],end[j]), sigma);

Obviously still not ideal. And it won't be quite as fast as yours (but
then I don't know what the speed diff will be or if it matters).

- Bob
